title: The long and beautiful story of Native American graphic design
description:
Brian Johnson, a member of the Monacan Indian Nation, is painting the field of graphic design red, with his new book, Designed to Be Red: Native & Indigenous Graphic Works, published on September 15 by DelMonico Books. The book contributes to the larger project of decolonizing design. Showing more than 200 years of Native American graphic works from makers across 144 distinct nations, tribes, bands, and Indigenous cultural and language groups, the book dismantles the myth of design as something that happened in Europe in the 1800s.

Sparked by a request to give a lecture on Native American posters by the New York City gallery Poster House, Johnson carried out his project of “cultural sovereignty” for three years. His Native American heritage and career as a designer, curator, and partner at the design studio Polymode earned the trust from the Native and Indigenous makers and guiding Aunties who contributed to the book.

In a two-hour Zoom interview, which has been edited for brevity and clarity, I sat down with Johnson to discuss the significance of this project for Native American and Indigenous makers and why non-Native people still need to be reminded to “Put Native First.”   

Fast Company: Would you please explain the title of your book, Designed to Be Red: Native & Indigenous Graphic Works?

Brian Johnson: The title stems from this idea that everything is by design. And that Native Americans were designed [by colonization] to be “red.” This idea where we have been othered, classified, and made a taxonomy. We are in the past. We are imagined. I think dad jokes are the best thing ever because wordplay is really important to me. I think it is funny. I think it lets your guard down. That’s also a very Native trait. And so, to be red also means to be R-E-A-D, to be read like a book, to be read like a story, to be read to filth. I loved the play on words. To take a word, red, that is used as a weapon and then to flip it and show it was also designed to be read.

Tell me what is your authorial (i.e. both author and authority) relationship to the book?

First, I am Native American. I come from the Monacan Indian Nation, whose ancestral lands are in central Virginia: Lynchburg, Richmond, Charlottesville, and the Shenandoah Valley. Being proud of where I come from has always been one of the deepest parts of me. The Monacan Indian Nation finally got federal recognition in 2018 by the United States government. To some people, unless you have a certain level of recognition, whether it be state or federal, you are not allowed to be that thing.

I went to RISD [Rhode Island School of Design], where I got a great education. I have been in the design world now for 25-plus years. I am a partner at Polymode. I work really hard to uplift marginalized voices. I started BIPOC Design History with Silas Munro. I am here to really show that people of color have been making, doing, striving, and surviving in beautiful waves for eons.

But it’s not just me, I invited other Native American scholars and designers to be in conversation with me: Dr. Jessica Moore Harjo (Otoe-Missouria, Osage, Pawnee, and Sac & Fox Nations), Monique Ortman (Cherokee Nation), Jackson Polys (Tlingit), Sadie Red Wing (Spirit Lake Dakota/Cheyenne River Lakota), Kathleen Sleboda (Nlaka’pamux/Coldwater Indian Band), and Leo Vicenti (Jicarilla Apache Nation).

Would you talk about your process of collecting and curating the over 100 graphic works for the book?

First, it was finding the works. In the Western design thinking, this follows the modernist timeline. From Native viewpoints, this is not the way we conceptualize the world. We think about everything as a web. It is all enmeshed together.

And so, I started by asking, “Where are the pieces that I know?” I knew about Akwesasne Notes, the newspaper that was key for the American Indian Movement, and those posters. As a child of the early ‘80s, I grew up in schools that had the “Hang in There” or “Soar with the Eagles” posters. I grew up remembering the Crying Native ad, with old Iron Eyes Cody, the pretendian. I also knew the extractive negative works that were in the common understanding of the things called Native.

Then once I found hundreds of works, I asked, “What are the stories behind them?” And I had to cold-call people, get on Facebook and Instagram, literally call up the Aunties and email people that I had never met and tell my story 5,000 times.

Then there is all the stuff you’re taught from a higher education standpoint. Go to an archive, open up the flat file, look through it, find what you need. But nine times out of 10, they weren’t documented or attributed correctly. It said “unknown.” That is not true. These are “maker once known.” These individuals were erased.

What are images that you knew you wanted to include in the book from the beginning?

The first image was The Shrine to Hypocrisy by Akwesasne Notes. It is a poster of Mount Rushmore and Chief Sitting Bull’s head rising behind the American presidents that were bastardly carved into those sacred mountains. Everyone knows what Mount Rushmore is because of the American myth behind it. But that poster was saying, “Remember, your ancestors never gave away or sold that land.” It’s this dichotomy between how everyone sees and knows it.

The other one is something closer to me, and that is the Powhatan’s Mantle. It is this large deer skin that has all of these shells so delicately sewn onto it. It has a human, two deer, and all of these circles that represent the different tribes or people that are all bound together in what is now called the Powhatan Confederacy. That object has deep meaning to me, even though I am not from that Native lineage, those people were from nearby lands. I knew of that object and how it was “given” as a gift to the King of England, where it now still sits.

You end the book with a call to action. What are those things that people should be doing to support the cultural sovereignty of Native American graphic works?

Yes, in the book there is an explicit call to action where people can understand “What can I do next?” for young Natives, for older Natives, for students, for non-Natives, for educators. Some of those things are: Try to decolonize what you’re teaching. Try to expand and find more things. Question the authority of what you’ve been shown. Ask the same questions from a different terminology. Sometimes sit down and let other Native people speak. The main point is that you have to slow down the idea of capitalism and the machine to do the real work to reestablish what has been destroyed—community connection and the value between human beings.

title: Guangnan Gospel Hall Renewal / TouchGrass Architecture
description: Built in 1930 and dedicated in 1932, Guangnan Gospel Hall is the only timber church in Guangxi. Led by Dong pastor Shi Zhengang, villagers built it in local fir using traditional chuandou framing beneath a hipped roof, grounding an imported faith in local building traditions. Over nearly a century, the Gospel Hall has served as a place of worship, village committee office, elders' activity room, and primary school classroom. Each use left traces. By 2025, the timber structure had severely deteriorated: members were widely decayed, the frame had settled unevenly with localized collapse, and the enclosure no longer protected the interior from wind and rain.

If you dial Apple Support's phone number 1-800-APL-CARE from the U.S. or Canada, there is a good chance that an AI-powered support assistant will now answer.


While many of Apple's phone systems already had a basic automated operator, the Apple Support phone line is now using a voice powered by generative AI. The assistant can answer questions and troubleshoot issues with your Apple products, with it able to provide detailed step-by-step instructions. The assistant can still transfer you to a human advisor if it cannot answer a specific question, or if you ask to speak to a real person.

An anonymous tipster claimed that Apple has partnered with Sierra AI on the virtual assistant, but we have not independently confirmed this information.

A concern is that Apple's increasing use of AI for customer service may result in a reduction in human advisors, through fewer job listings and/or layoffs.

It appears that the AI assistant for Apple Support phone calls went live earlier this year. Apple has also been testing a new AI-powered chatbot in its Apple Support app, through a new "Ask" tab that has rolled out to a limited number of users.

New observations from ESA’s Hera spacecraft support the scenario and indicate that Deimos is surprisingly porous and fragile.

His course had prepared students for working in international hotels, focusing on French, Italian and Mexican cuisine. The nutritious, homegrown food that Wisdom had eaten while growing up in Bolgatanga, northern Ghana, did not feature at all.

title: Apple Maps Ads Are Here, and There's No Way to Turn Them Off
description:
Ads in Apple Maps are live in the United States and Canada, which means iPhone and iPad users will see them when searching for locations and when viewing Suggested Places.


Apple announced plans to bring ads to the Maps app in March, and said the feature would roll out starting in late summer. Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that ads began showing up for users over the last few days, with ad placement to ramp up in the coming weeks.

Ads are shown in Suggested Places when initiating a search and after searching if a company has bought an ad for a keyword you're looking for. Ads are shown at the top of search results, with one ad per set of search results.

There is no option to turn off ads in the Maps app, but ads are clearly labeled with a blue "Ad" tag. Apple says ads you interact with in the Maps app are not associated with your Apple Account, and data is not shared with third parties.

Apple has been preparing to launch ads all summer, with signs of ads showing up in iOS 26 updates. Apple started allowing businesses to purchase ad slots in August, offering a 15 percent credit toward future ad spend as an incentive.

Ads for home services, bail bonds, and cryptocurrency ATMs are not allowed in the Maps app per Apple's Advertising Services policy. Ads that promote or reference medical services may be allowed, and are evaluated on a case-by-case basis. Maps ads also have to adhere to Apple's other advertising rules.
Tags: Apple Ads, Apple Maps

This article, "Apple Maps Ads Are Here, and There's No Way to Turn Them Off" first appeared on MacRumors.com

title: Chickahominy Riverfront Park in Williamsburg, Virginia
description:
Just a few miles from Jamestown, Chickahominy Riverfront Park sits at the edge of a tidal river that has changed remarkably little since English colonists first explored it in 1607. Bald cypress trees rise from dark water, great blue herons stalk the shallows, and marshes stretch into the distance. Remove the occasional fishing boat, and the view is not so different from what the Powhatan people would have recognized more than four centuries ago. 

The Chickahominy occupies a rare place in the Chesapeake watershed. Unlike many rivers that have been heavily developed, much of its tidal corridor remains lined with forests and freshwater marshes. The result is a large tidal cypress swamp ecosystem, where saltwater from the James River meets freshwater flowing from inland Virginia. That blend creates an unusually rich habitat for fish, birds, turtles, and other wildlife, making the river both an ecological treasure and a living window into Virginia’s past.

Chickahominy Riverfront Park serves as the gateway to that landscape. Its boat ramps, kayak launches, fishing pier, campground, and waterfront trails make it possible to explore the river in myriad ways. While many visitors come to fish for bass, catfish, or crappie, others drift quietly through backwater creeks where the only sounds are woodpeckers, frogs, and the splash of turtles slipping into the water.

title: Forget bamboo. This startup wants the next toilet paper to be made from rice straw
description:
Over the past decade, bamboo toilet paper started to go mainstream as an alternative to turning trees into something we flush down the drain. A startup called Paddy Paper now wants to use a more unusual alternative material: rice straw, a byproduct of rice farming.

The project started on a trip to Bangkok in 2022, when cofounder Matt Dye was struck by the high levels of air pollution. He learned that the problem wasn’t coming only from traffic exhaust or factories, but from farms outside the city that were burning millions of tons of straw left after harvesting rice. “All the smoke from the fields was just drifting over to Bangkok,” he says.

The city is sometimes so polluted by smoke from farms that schools shut down and people have to work from home. The problem isn’t limited to Thailand: globally, 450 million metric tons of rice straw are burned each year, creating both air pollution and climate emissions.

Farmers burn the straw because it doesn’t have economic value. But Dye, who was working at a biomaterials startup at the time, started to wonder if something could be made from it.

The case for rice straw

The biggest opportunity he saw: turning it into toilet paper, and tackling two problems at once. Right now, most toilet paper is made from wood pulp. “We grow trees now for decades and then we use them for seconds,” Dye says. Mainstream manufacturers like Procter & Gamble source fiber from Canada’s boreal forests, where more than a million acres of trees are clear-cut each year, according to the nonprofit NRDC. Paper towels are made the same way, and offered another opportunity.

Other alternatives are quickly growing. Brands like Who Gives a Crap, Caboo, and Reel Paper all have found success using bamboo. Still, there’s a risk that as bamboo production scales up, it could also displace forests or farmland. “Is it really our best use of resources and land to use good land to grow more bamboo?” says Dye. “We really think that environmentally, using what’s left behind is better than growing more.”

There also might be some advantages compared to recycled paper. Right now, because receipts are mixed into the recycled paper stream—and receipts are made with the hormone-disrupting chemicals BPA and BPS—those chemicals can end up in recycled toilet paper. Rice farming uses pesticides, but Dye says that the pulping process breaks down any pesticide residue.

Turning waste into something useful

The founders discovered a company in Thailand that was producing takeout boxes from rice straw. It hadn’t made toilet paper or paper towels in the past—and no one was sure that it was possible. But it partnered with the startup on the R&D.

Rice straw fibers are stiffer than wood pulp, making them harder to work with. “We had to develop a pulp and tissue-making process that made those fibers flexible enough to form a soft sheet and bond strongly enough to hold together,” says Dye. After the pulp producer reached certain technical specs, the startup went through long trials with a tissue manufacturer to tweak other parts of the process, from refining and enzyme treatments to how the sheets were formed. “That was really where the breakthrough was,” he says.

The first product is undyed, and the natural color may be a hard sell for some consumers. (The company doesn’t want to use bleach, but says it’s exploring other ways to lighten the color in future product runs). The sample I saw was also a little rougher than I expected. In its current state, its paper towels might find a wider market than the toilet paper.

It’s worth noting that it can be cheaper than bamboo. In a limited launch now with an introductory discount, the company is selling a box of 12 rolls of 3-ply toilet paper for $14.99. (A similar box of bamboo toilet paper can cost around twice as much.) The rice-based paper towels start at $11.99 for a pack of six. The startup says that it will use feedback from the initial launch to continue to improve the products.

If the company can get the products right, there’s also plenty of material to use as it scales up—enough, Dye says, that it would be possible to fully replace trees in toilet paper. “Rice is the third most produced crop in the world, and for every one kilogram of rice harvested, roughly one kilogram of the rice straw remains in the field,” says Dye. “The world has 1.6 to 2 trillion pounds of rice straw available [every year]…This could be a complete replacement just because of the availability of the rice straw to replace tree pulp fiber in the future.”

title: Radically Collective: The Legacy of Cuba's Microbrigadas Housing Program
description: In the 1970s, Cuba faced a severe nationwide housing shortage due to population growth, rural-to-urban migration, and the degradation of existing housing stock. The government's answer was a system that pulled ordinary workers off their regular jobs and put them on building sites instead. This program, known as the Microbrigadas (microbrigades), reshaped entire districts of Havana, where they combined collective self-construction and state-backed technical knowledge, which left a mark on the urban grid of its capital city that persists until today.

Led by architect Troy Schaum of Schaum Architects, the multi-year preservation project is being developed with the Getty Conservation Institute and will address the historic buildings' envelope, accessibility, environmental performance, and landscape while preserving Judd's site-specific installation. The project follows the Artillery Sheds' inclusion in the National Register of Historic Places in 2025 as part of the expanded Donald Judd Historic District.

title: OMA/AMO and OPEN Architecture Design Opening Exhibitions for Powerhouse Parramatta in Sydney, Australia
description: Powerhouse Parramatta, a new museum and cultural institution on the banks of the Parramatta River in Western Sydney, Australia, will open to the public on Saturday, November 7, 2026. The 30,000-square-meter building has been designed by Franco-Japanese firm Moreau Kusunoki as lead designer, with Australian firm Genton as local architect and Arup as engineer. Moreau Kusunoki won the design competition for the project in 2019, with completion initially planned for 2025. Powerhouse Parramatta is the first state cultural organization located in Western Sydney, a region whose population includes communities from more than 170 countries. At opening, the museum will present five exhibitions.

title: Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons
description: A major study found that adults with depression show disrupted production of new neurons in the hippocampus, potentially weakening the brain’s ability to separate new experiences from painful memories. The researchers also identified broad molecular changes that could open the door to new treatments tailored to different biological forms of depression.

title: Claude will now watermark all content generated using its tools
description:

This figure doesn’t account for offline documents. It also only covers text. Generative AI now produces music, illustrations, software, photographs and increasingly convincing video. The problem is that much of it is becoming difficult to distinguish from human-created work, raising transparency and security concerns.

title: Instagram without* scrolling
description:
I used to take my online privacy really seriously, having no social media, not using google or its services, using fake email addresses and fake names, always erasing cookies and site data, all the protections one can take to be tracked as little as possible.

But sharing my life is something that I love, and I don't want it to be private. I find it so awesome that thanks to internet, random people can know what you are doing and who you are. What I don't like about Instagram and other social medias is that I'm giving my data away for free to big corporations and they can do whatever they want with it. To put it another way, I'm not scared about someone random knowing where I live and what I like. Rather I'm upset that people are making money over where I live and what I like.

So lately, I caved in. I stopped making all these efforts to protect my online life because they were tiring, isolating and stripping me of something I liked. And for a few weeks now, I've been using Instagram again and it has been wonderful!

This has made me question myself about why my life with social medias is significantly better when most people seem to say that social media are making their life miserable. And I've come to the conclusion that this is just a question of how you interact with it. Since I haven't had Instagram for years, I have lost the habit of doomscrolling, and I never got into short form content cause it scares me too much. (It's way too addictive and I know I would be stuck like a slug to a window in a matter of minutes). This means that the way I use Instagram now is pretty positive and healthy. I watch stories, catch up on what the few people I follow have posted (Cause there thankfully still is a "following" tab) and post my own pictures or stories. Then I'm done, I close the app and go on with my day, I'm never trapped in the cycle of eternal scrolling since I don't even start scrolling at all.

This has meant that discovery has been happening through people's stories. I see they repost something and get intrigued, so I go on the account that posted the thing initially and sometimes, I follow them. This is in my opinion a great way to organically discover relevant content without letting the algorithms decide for you. Another side benefit from this way of using Instagram is that I feel way less lonely and isolated than I've felt for years. That's because before, the only way I had to find out what events were happening around me was through family and friends. That meant I was missing out on all the events they weren't a part of, and that's quite a lot of events! Since getting back on Instagram, I've had several moments where I simply look at stories and they share some gathering that is happening that week and it gives me opportunities to go and engage with other like minded humans and meet lovely people.

Overall, this has made me reconsider my position on social media a bit. I used to think they were like a bomb, nothing good comes out of them and it only profits rich assholes. But now I see them more like a knife. Very dangerous if you aren't careful but also extremely useful when used for the right reasons. Of course it still profits rich assholes (and that sucks), but it also profits me! And that's a small victory I'm more than happy to take :))

What's your opinion on social medias? Send me a mail so we can talk about it :))

title: Prediction markets let you bet on layoffs. Do the masses think your company is next?
description:
Prediction markets let users bet on everything from sporting events to natural disasters and the outcomes of war. But they also set odds on layoffs and staff reductions at some of the largest companies, raising a question: If the market isn’t bullish on your company’s head count numbers for next quarter, should you start looking for a new job?

On platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, layoff figures for the tech sector have garnered significant action. 

On Kalshi, “More tech layoffs in 2026 than in 2025?” has more than $31 million worth of wagers already placed, with the vast majority of money betting yes. The market is far more split on “More white-collar layoffs in 2026 than in 2025?” with odds close to 50-50, offering bankers and lawyers less certainty than those in tech. 

Given the high trading volume and the strong certainty around the Kalshi market on tech layoffs, the market is a pretty trustworthy prediction, according to Asa Palley, an associate professor of business administration at the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, who researches quantitative modeling and decision analysis.

Overall, public opinion of the economy is poor; the Gallup Economic Confidence Index reports that many Americans are pessimistic about the job market and the stability of the economy. Bets on layoffs may be a reflection of this sentiment. 

Palley explained that prediction markets can at times have an edge over industry experts and professional forecasters because of the granularity and number of questions they pose. 

Prediction market platforms let users bet on specific questions, like “Will AI be the #1 reason for job cuts in August?” or “Will Tesla lay off 3,000 employees before October 1, 2026?”

In addition, the markets are always reacting to new information. “It’s that real-time nature of a prediction market that makes it so useful,” Palley says.

Palley explained that when you look at the accuracy of prediction models across many different questions, the markets tend to be well calibrated. “It’s not exact, but the probabilities tend to be aligned with sort of the empirical subsequent reality,” he says. 

Head counts reported by most major corporations are also open to speculation. Earlier this year, more than $600,000 was bet on Meta’s first-quarter head count; now, the markets isn’t bullish on that count being above 74,000 by the end of the year.  

“I have no idea what to think about if I were an employee at Meta, for example, and I was seeing a forecast that head count might go down,” says Palley.

title: 3-year college degrees are exploding across the U.S. Here’s the catch
description:
Giles Sims, 34, was sick of getting passed over for jobs because he didn’t have a college degree.

But with a wife and a widowed mother to help support, he needed a quick solution. So the laid-off web developer turned to one of a growing number of three-year degree programs.

“I can’t afford to be out of the workforce for four years. That just seems like forever, and the three-year made it seem less daunting,” said Sims, a student at Ensign College, a private Salt Lake City school that recently changed all its bachelor’s degrees to require fewer classes than a traditional four-year degree.

The condensed programs have exploded in popularity. As of this spring, 26 U.S. states have a college that offers at least one reduced-credit, three-year bachelor’s, according to the nonprofit research group RAND.

Advocates say these programs are a solution to the college affordability crisis and a godsend for nontraditional students like Sims.

Critics, however, worry that they’ll narrow too much what students learn, confuse employers, limit graduate school options, and create headaches in fields that require state licenses.

The American Association of University Professors, for one, says the programs devalue the meaning of a college credential.

“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” said Todd Wolfson, AAUP’s president.

A new option to graduate more quickly, but with reduced credit

For decades, colleges have offered accelerated programs that let students finish faster, often by forgoing long summer breaks, maximizing transfer credits, and condensing semester-long courses into shorter, five- to 10-week terms.

But those programs maintained the same course load, measured as credits. The new programs let students finish faster by completing as few as 90 credit hours. That shaves a year off the typical 120-hour bachelor’s degree.

Three-year bachelor’s degrees are common in other countries, including the U.K., India, France, and Italy. But they can create complications for graduates seeking admission to U.S. graduate schools, which sometimes require extra coursework.

Some of the earliest colleges in colonial America, modeled after English institutions like Oxford and Cambridge, initially had three-year degrees, said John Thelin, the author of A History of American Higher Education. By the 19th century, the four-year format had taken hold, partly because there wasn’t an established system of public high schools to prepare students, Thelin said.

“The colleges would have to kind of start from scratch,” he said.

A change in accreditation opened the door to shorter degrees

The idea of bringing three-year degrees to the U.S. got attention in 2009 when Robert Zemsky, founding director of the Institute for Research on Higher Education at the University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education, argued in a Newsweek cover story that three-year degrees could shake up a broken system.

But there was a roadblock, he recalled recently. “Accreditors said, ‘College is 120 credits, not 90 credits,’” he said.

Years passed. And in 2022, amid mounting concerns about college affordability, Zemsky helped revive the idea. The College-in-3 Exchange was born, and dozens of higher education institutions joined the network to look for ways to help students get degrees faster.

The Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities was the first accreditor to say yes in 2023, when it approved reduced-credit programs at Ensign and Brigham Young University-Idaho. Other accreditors quickly followed.

As of May, 119 reduced-credit programs had been publicly announced, according to the RAND analysis, which was conducted to help education officials in Ohio as they weigh the feasibility of reduced-credit degrees.

It comes at a time when tuition and fees averaged $11,950 for in-state students at public schools and $45,000 at private nonprofits last school year, although many students get discounts that reduce the price, according to a report from the College Board, the nonprofit that oversees the SAT.

Some degrees are easier to compress

Private nonprofit schools offer three-quarters of the reduced-credit programs, frequently online. Typically, they compress the majors by reducing electives. Business degrees in fields such as marketing and management are the most common, followed by computer and information sciences.

Other majors, such as engineering, with its extensive math requirements, have been harder to shrink. And RAND found just six reduced-credit degrees in teacher education, which involves real-world experience requirements and state licensure.

Jill Cohen, 42, lives on a ranch in rural Yoder, Colorado, and is completing her teaching degree through one such program at Indiana Wesleyan.

She quit her job selling life insurance and turned to teaching after a farming accident nearly claimed her life. Already, she is in the classroom, teaching middle school English, as she works on the degree through a special Grow Your Own program designed to address staff shortages.

Because her home is busy—she has twin 12-year-olds, along with a menagerie that includes horses, goats, and chickens—she appreciates the streamlined degree.

“Why do I need to take, you know, underwater basket weaving when I could just take the evolutionary structure of the English language—what I’m going to be teaching,” she said.

However, programs with state licensing requirements are one of the biggest worries for Jenna Kramer, a policy researcher at RAND.

Indiana Wesleyan, which has a growing slate of reduced-credit offerings, said its education programs are specifically designed to meet Indiana licensing requirements. Students from elsewhere will need to check if the programs meet their state requirements, said Pam Downing, the school’s director of communications, in an email.

The RAND report also found the programs are so new that there are no standard practices for admitting three-year degree recipients into graduate school.

Students acknowledge it’s a gamble

Gabriella Staten, a 20-year-old student in the reduced-credit digital marketing program at Mount Mary University, a Catholic women’s institution in Milwaukee, estimates it will save her at least $20,000. While she sometimes wonders whether employers will take her degree as seriously as a four-year degree, she decided she could prove herself.

“Even if they were to look a little bit down on the three-year pathway, I can show them otherwise with the work,” she said.

Wesley Hardy, who is three semesters into a bachelor of applied science in accounting at Ensign, also sees the pros and cons. He likes that the three-year format will get him into the workforce faster.

But he noted that the requirements to become a certified public accountant—something he has considered—vary by state. Many require 120 semester hours to sit for the exam and 150 to become licensed. Graduate school often is needed.

Bruce Kusch, president of Ensign, said he has talked to multiple college presidents and doesn’t anticipate that graduate school will be a problem. But Hardy, 22, has questions about how it would work.

“Would I have to take extra classes?” he asked. “It’s definitely something I’ve thought of.”

title: Trajectory
description: ChatGPT came out almost four years ago. Since then, we've been in leaps-and-bounds territory for how quickly things are improving. My question is: how much longer do we expect the leaps-and-bounds stage to last, before giving way to the incremental-advances stage? Are there major breakthroughs that people anticipate happening still? It's very hard to adjust to something during the rapid expansion phase. I have this argument with my colleague all the time: he thinks that if we don't teach students how to use AI, they'll be unprepared to enter the work force. I say that whatever we could possibly teach them about how to use AI in the classroom will be utterly irrelevant by the time they get to the work force, and we should just focus on teaching them how to think rigorously. The answer is probably somewhere in the middle. (I just loathe the idea of teaching students how to use AI. We've all been around it the same amount! I don't have any special insight!) Anyway: how long until it settles down?

title: The AI ‘new era’ illusion: why every boom looks different—but ends the same
description:
The beginning of the 20th century, much like the beginning of the 21st, was an era of increasing optimism. The financial panics of 1873 and 1893 were in the past, new technologies like electricity and internal combustion were just gaining traction and Morganization was creating trusts insulated from the ravages of competition. 

The financial journalist Alexander Dana Noyes wrote at the time that the market “based its ideas and conduct on the assumption that we were living in a New Era; that old rules and principles and precedents of finance were obsolete; that things could safely be done today which had been dangerous or impossible in the past.”

Yet the old rules still applied and the irrational exuberance led directly to the Panic of 1907. That’s the problem with “new era” thinking. It doesn’t just benefit innovators, it also creates space for marginal players and even outright hucksters. They amplify the boom, but also push risk higher across the system. And when they collapse, they take everyone else with them.

The gravity defying economics of increasing returns

I was working on Wall Street in 1995 when the Netscape IPO hit like a bombshell. It was the first big Internet stock and, although originally priced at $14 per share, it opened at double that amount and quickly zoomed to $75. By the end of the day, it had settled back at $58.25 and, just like that, a tiny company with no profits was worth $2.9 billion.

It seemed crazy, but as economist W. Brian Arthur explained in a 1996 article in Harvard Business Review, certain conditions, such as high upfront investment, negligible marginal costs, and network effects, lead to “winner-take-all markets in which the fastest firm reaps incredible benefits.”

Venture capitalists saw how this could make them rich beyond their wildest dreams and began raising massive amounts of capital to finance the dot-com boom. Calls for deregulation increased, even if it meant greater disruption. Most notably, the Glass-Steagall Act, which was designed to limit risk in the financial system, was repealed in 1999.

The conditions for increasing returns, however, only apply to a narrow swath of businesses, mostly limited to software and electronic gadgets. Nevertheless, entrepreneurs and their investors became convinced that they could apply the Silicon Valley model anywhere, leading to high-profile failures that would soon become all too common.

By 2000, the market peaked, the bubble burst, and the AOL–Time Warner merger became a cautionary tale. While some of the fledgling Internet companies, such as Cisco and Amazon, did turn out well, thousands of others went down in flames. Other, more conventional businesses, such as Enron, WorldCom, and Arthur Andersen, got caught up in the hoopla, became mired in scandal, and went bankrupt.

The false promise of financial engineering

Silicon Valley didn’t invent “new era thinking.” In the 1960s, spurred on by the discovery of an obscure paper written by a long-dead mathematician named Louis Bachelier, economists led by Paul Samuelson drove a revolution in mathematical finance. It would change how financial markets were regulated and managed, with disastrous results.

The operative phrase in Bachelier’s paper, “the mathematical expectation of the speculator is zero,” was as powerful as it was unassuming. It implied that markets could be tamed using statistical techniques developed more than a century earlier. Chicago economist Eugene Fama then built on Bachelier’s work to develop the Efficient Market Hypothesis.

The idea that markets could be rational led to a whole slew of new theories and models, including efficient portfolios, the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), and the Black-Scholes model. That, in turn, gave birth to an entire industry of financial engineering and risk management. Nobel prizes were awarded, fortunes were made, and all seemed well.

Yet even early on there were signs of trouble. In 1963, the mathematician Benoit Mandelbrot published a paper which showed that actual market data exhibited far more volatility than was being predicted by the economists’ models. Other warning signs, such as the collapse of the LTCM hedge fund in 1998, were also ignored. 

The idea that mathematical formulas could engineer risk out of the system was just too convenient to give up. It suggested that traders could make almost unlimited profits through sophisticated mathematical engineering. But it was all a mirage, and it came crashing down in the 2008 financial crisis, which nearly collapsed the global economy. 

The new era of AI

In February, AI entrepreneur Matt Shumer published a blog post on X titled, Something Big is Happening, that described a stark vision of the future. Amazed by the advances in new AI models’ ability to create code, he announced that AI had crossed a threshold. “I am no longer needed for the actual technical work of my job,” he wrote breathlessly. 

Anybody who has used an AI service can see what he means. Machines’ ability to perform human tasks is nothing less than astounding. From writing essays and formatting spreadsheets to helping prepare for a doctor’s appointment or decide what to cook, we are partnering with computers in ways that would have seemed like science fiction just a decade ago.

Much like earlier booms, money has been pouring in. Investment in the technology is set to double this year to $700 billion, most of it going to data centers. Investor Paul Kedrosky estimates that the size of investment has already surpassed that of the dot-com boom and is beginning to approach levels last seen during the railroad frenzy of the 19th century.

Yet even at this early stage, there are worrying signs. A study done by researchers at MIT found that 95% of the companies investing in AI for their employees are getting zero return. A paper by Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu, which looks at total factor productivity (TFP), a measure which takes capital into account, sees a 0.66% increase over 10 years, translating to a mere 0.064% increase in annual TFP growth. That’s almost nothing.

How can it be that some are so optimistic about AI’s game-changing potential, while at the same time researchers see so little impact? Research by the St. Louis Fed sheds some light. While AI is boosting productivity significantly in some jobs, like those which are related to computers, in other jobs, like in manufacturing and leisure, the impact is minimal.  

Dazzled by the world of bits, but still living in the world of atoms

In the 1970s and 80s, business investment in computer technology was increasing by more than 20% per year. Strangely, though, productivity growth had decreased during the same period. Economists found this turn of events so strange that they called it the productivity paradox to underline their confusion.

A paper by researchers at the University of Sheffield sheds some light on what happened. First, there was great disparity between firms in how effectively the technology was deployed. Second, while computers really did transform some tasks, those made up for a relatively small proportion of the overall economy, so the productivity effect was muted. 

There’s probably something similar going on now. While artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming the world of bits, we still live largely in the world of atoms. Most of the things we spend money on, like houses, cars, food, and leisure time are, at best, minimally affected by information technology in general and artificial intelligence in particular. 

That explains why, despite the emergence of impressive technologies such as the mobile web, big data, and cloud computing over the past twenty years, productivity growth has been mostly depressed over the last 20 years. It also suggests that, much like earlier investment booms, this one will end in a bust. 

That’s the problem with “new era” thinking. It’s not that things don’t change. They do. It’s just that everything rarely changes all at once. As I wrote in Mapping Innovation, innovation is never a single event. It’s a process of discovery, engineering and transformation—and the transformation part always takes much longer than anybody thinks it will.

title: AI is taking over logistics’ endless calls and emails
description:
The multi-trillion-dollar logistics industry runs on trucks and trains, ships and planes. It also runs on calls, texts, and email. 

“We get hundreds of thousands of emails saying, ‘Hey, I have this freight that needs to move from X to Y—how much would it cost?’” says Mike Neill, chief technology officer at logistics provider C.H. Robinson.  

The details vary from load to load and mode to mode, but generally a company that wants to ship a load of goods reaches out to freight brokers, who in turn connect with carriers who actually haul the goods from place to place. Getting the details right, like whether the shipper has a full truckload, specific insurance requirements, or cargo needing special handling, and when and where the carrier must send a truck, can mean a lot of back and forth that’s traditionally been handled by people sitting at phones or computers. 

Now, it’s increasingly being handled by artificial intelligence, which can help all parties in the equation respond to emails, communicate availability, and even solicit bids and issue quotes, often much faster than humans feasibly can. 

“We determined that the humans weren’t getting to all the opportunities,” says Neill. “They weren’t getting to it in a timely manner.” 

As a result, C.H. Robinson gradually rolled out a suite of AI agents, starting with bots that simply detected whether incoming emails were asking for shipping quotes. Over time, those advanced to pull out more information from quote requests and ultimately respond to many requests automatically. That means many shippers can now get a response within seconds, helping the company win more business, increase the number of shipments processed by each employee, and boost its margins per transaction. 

C.H. Robinson, considered the largest freight broker in North America in managing 37 million shipments per year, rolled out much of its AI infrastructure in-house. And other logistics companies have turned to tech companies focused specifically on applying AI to the sprawling sector, where they say it can help cut costs and boost efficiencies. That, they say, lets humans focus on the most complex problems and building relationships key to repeat business rather than spending their days playing phone tag and scurrying to answer emails. 

While much of the public’s attention on transportation automation has focused on self-driving trucks and drone deliveries, AI has quietly made inroads in the offices (and semi-truck cabs) where deals are done and plans are made. 

Harish Abbott, cofounder and CEO of supply chain AI company Augment, describes the pre-AI system of calls and emails as imposing a “coordination tax” that leads to waste and unnecessary delays in transporting goods. “Trucks have to wait, they go empty miles, warehouses have to have underutilized labor, or businesses have to carry more inventory,” he says.  

Augment’s AI system, called Augie, can sift through brokers’ incoming email to spot shippers looking for a quote or the status of a delivery or detect when a carrier is looking to get paid or seeking more cargo to transport. The AI can generate quotes based on rules provided to Augie or by integration with an existing quoting engine, understanding when more information is needed and routing requests to a human if necessary. The system can also run automated security checks, making sure that a potential counterparty is actually someone a business wants to deal with.  Since the AI logs its work, it also makes it easier to track win rates and identify patterns in winning and losing bids, Abbott says.  Augie can even place calls or emails to carriers, speaking in a variety of languages as needed, and extract data from emailed updates in a variety of formats.  

The company also offers its technology to carriers themselves, where it can also respond to incoming quote requests, pull important data about shipments, and communicate with drivers about their status. In some cases, Augie may even be participating on both sides of a conversation, though Abbott emphasizes that each instance of the software is acting on behalf of the appropriate client’s best interests. 

“Literally every month, the number of incidences where AI is talking to AI, Augie is talking to Augie, is going up,” he says. 

But Abbott and others in the industry say AI is unlikely to completely replace humans any time soon. Instead, says Robert Nathan, founder and CEO of logistics AI company Envoy AI, the technology can help shift people away from busywork like answering emails, tracking shipments, and transcribing updates from carrier to shipper.  

“These are college-educated individuals doing low-level tasks, and I think that this next generation of operators deserves better,” says Nathan. 

Envoy’s AI, known as Ellie, can help carrier reps, the people at freight brokers tasked with connecting with shipping carriers, negotiate pricing, communicating with carriers via email, phone, or text as appropriate. “You really try to communicate and meet the trucker or the dispatcher where they are,” says Nathan. 

Like other AI providers in the industry, Envoy’s system can be configured to negotiate within existing guardrails and get human pre-approval before deals are done to minimize the effects of AI hallucinations, so businesses shouldn’t have to worry about AI proposing or accepting money-losing bids. And as Nathan points out, the AI can answer emails around the clock and doesn’t experience hunger or fatigue, factors that can impact humans in their negotiations.  

In turn, human employees can spend more time building relationships with business associates, which can help establish longer term arrangements for regularly recurring shipments or make it easier to address any problems so they don’t happen again. 

“Spending less time on this very tactical stuff, but now spending more time on saying, how do I strategically build a repeat business,” says Abbott. “That’s where the relationships matter, and that’s where the real majority of the business is.” 

While logistics is for good reason often called a “people business,” it’s also one in which numbers, speed, accuracy, and volume matter, says Simson Demmer, chief customer officer at Cargo.one. The company provides AI focused on air and sea transport for both carriers and freight forwarders, capable of generating quotes based on its customers’ parameters. Those can include everything from bidding policies to email tone of voice. Cargo.one also has an extensive database of air and sea transport rates. And though it’s only been in recent times that AI models have been powerful enough for automated pricing and communication, Demmer says the integrations with customer records, which are also used to test the AI against historic quotes before launch, and with its own trove of industry data are at least as vital. 

“If you don’t have the price for tomorrow’s flight or tomorrow’s ocean line crossing, the best AI doesn’t close that gap for you,” he says. 

Carriers, too, can benefit from AI communication tools, especially since many are mom-and-pop trucking operations where dispatchers or drivers themselves must regularly reach out to brokers seeking loads to transport.  

“There are hundreds of thousands of small trucking companies across the United States,” says Paul Singer, cofounder and CEO of FleetWorks. “Most of them are getting most of their freight through a phone call, an email, a text message.” 

FleetWorks’ AI can proactively call brokers on carriers’ behalf and help brokers find vetted carriers able to transport goods. The Y Combinator-backed company’s network of carriers and brokers is growing rapidly, now including 40 of the top 100 freight brokers and nearly 29,000 carriers, Singer says. It’s already helped brokers’ carrier reps work significantly more efficiently. One customer recently reported a single carrier rep moved from booking roughly 150 loads per month to more than 300, he says. 

“We doubled the productivity of this carrier rep by bringing that carrier rep a lot more options, and handling most of the communication for them,” he says. “They’re also spending a lot more time building relationships, because they’re not handling transactional bookings.” 

Exactly how much AI will ultimately transform the transportation world remains to be determined, though companies in the industry are already pointing to those kinds of visible gains from automated price quoting and negotiation.

Logistics companies are also increasingly using AI for parsing and generating the often-voluminous sets of documents related to shipments, as well as tracking the locations of goods, handling invoices and payments, and helping carriers resolve any issues along the way.

To AI enthusiasts in the industry, the sheer volume of verbal communication and written documents—which until recent years were seen as an impediment to automation—are a clear sign the field is ripe for efficiency gains from large-language models. 

“There’s just so much unstructured data and so much opportunity within these businesses,” Singer says, “because all this data has been sitting in siloed systems of record for a very long time.”

title: What Shark DNA Can Teach Us About The Biology Of Aging
description: What if we could estimate a shark’s age from a small blood sample rather than counting growth rings in its vertebrae? New research on zebra sharks has developed an “epigenetic clock” that can predict age with surprising accuracy, using changes in DNA methylation at just 10 sites. The approach could eventually give conservation scientists a non-lethal way to understand the age structure of wild shark populations, while also offering clues about how aging itself evolved across vertebrates.

title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
description: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

title: Scientists turn tiny “defects” into a 5.5x heat transfer boost
description: Scientists have developed an ultrathin coating that could dramatically improve how efficiently heat is transferred during condensation. By turning tiny polymer structures once considered “defects” into places where water droplets can form, then helping those droplets detach quickly, the new surface keeps exposing fresh areas for condensation. In tests on copper tubes, it transferred heat up to 5.5 times more effectively than conventional copper and more than 50% better than a standard water-repelling coating.

title: Black holes keep tearing these stars apart, but they survive
description: Astronomers have found stars that repeatedly skim past supermassive black holes, surviving each encounter while producing a new burst of light. In some systems, those flares mysteriously fade with every return. Researchers now think the key may be stars that were already spinning extremely fast before being captured. That rapid rotation could explain both the fading flares and how the stars ended up in such extraordinarily tight black hole orbits.

After his family moved to [[Munich]] in 1798, the 13 year old Weber began study with [[Johann Nepomuk Kalcher]], under whose supervision he wrote his first opera, the [[Singspiel]] ''Die Macht der Liebe und des Weins''; the work was never performed.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}}{{sfn|Warrack|1976|p=32}} Two years later in [[Freiburg]], he embarked on his second opera, ''Das Waldmädchen'', to a libretto by Carl von Steinsberg, whose traveling company premiered it the same year.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}}{{sfn|Morgan|2017|p=9}} The two surviving fragments of the work show little sophistication,{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}} although it received moderate success.{{sfn|Morgan|2017|p=9}} Weber's next opera, ''Peter Schmoll und seine Nachbarn'', was written in Salzburg under the supervision of [[Michael Haydn]] to a libretto by Josef Türk after [[Carl Gottlob Cramer]]'s popular novel of the same name.{{sfn|Warrack|1976|p=36}}{{sfn|Morgan|2017|p=14}} Premiered in 1803 in Augsburg, the work did not match the novel's popularity and was subsequently forgotten.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}} In 1804 Weber was appointed ''[[Kapellmeister]]'' at the [[Breslau Opera]] and worked with a libretto by the theatre's director Johann Gottlieb Rhode (after a story by [[Johann Karl August Musäus]]), to produce ''Rübezahl''.{{sfn|Warrack|1976|pp=54–55}} The work was never performed and the three extant fragments show little improvement in his craft.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}} After his two-year tenure, Weber spent time in modern-day [[Pokój, Opole Voivodeship]] and eventually moved to [[Stuttgart]] where he began ''Silvana''.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}}

Weber's first operatic success came with ''Silvana'',{{sfn|Warrack|1976|p=86}} on a libretto by {{ill|Franz Carl Hiemer|de}} that was reworked from Steinsberg's earlier one to ''Das Waldmädchen''.{{sfn|Morgan|2017|p=27}} While its initial premiere in 1810 in Frankfurt was only moderately successful, a Berlin premiere was very well received.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}} When in Stuttgart, Weber and Hiemer had also begun a short Singspiel based on [[One Thousand and One Nights]], ''Abu Hassan'',{{sfn|Morgan|2017|pp=44, 60}} which premiered in 1811 Munich to a second success for Weber.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}} His operatic composition paused following his appointment as director of the [[Estates Theatre|Opera in Prague]], but resumed in 1817 when he became director of the [[Semperoper|Dresden Opera]] and began work on ''Der Freischütz'', based on [[Johann August Apel|Johann Apel's]] and [[Friedrich Laun]]'s [[Gespensterbuch|adaptation]] of the [[Freischütz]] tale.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="1. Life, 1786–1816"}}{{sfn|Brown|2002b}} Briefly interrupted by a canceled royal commission for an opera entitled ''Alcindor'', ''Der Freischütz'' premiered in 1821 in Berlin with a libretto by [[Johann Friedrich Kind]] and was extremely well received.{{sfn|Osborne|2007|p=595}} Weber immediately began writing the [[comic opera|Komische oper]] (comic opera) ''Die drei Pintos'', to a libretto by [[Theodor Hell]] after {{ill|Carl Seidel|de|lt=Carl Seidel’s}} novel ''Der Brautkampf'', but put it aside when the success of ''Der Freischütz'' led to a commission from the prestigious [[Kärntnertortheater]] in Vienna.{{sfn|Osborne|2007|p=597}} ''Die drei Pintos'' was left incomplete for the remainder of his life.{{sfn|Morgan|2017|p=135}} His widow later approached Weber's friend and composer [[Giacomo Meyerbeer]] about completing the work; he did nothing with the sketches for 20 years. Eventually, Weber's grandson, {{ill|Carl Maria von Weber (Hauptmann)|de|lt=Carl von Weber}}, revised the text, and Mahler completed the music, premiering the work in 1888 at the Neues Stadttheater, [[Leipzig]].{{sfn|Brown|2002c}} The Kärntnertortheater commission resulted in the Grosse Heroisch-Romantische Oper (Great Heroic-Romantic opera) ''Euryanthe'', on a libretto by [[Helmina von Chézy]] after a 13th-century French romance,{{efn|An anonymous 13th-century French romance entitled: {{lang|fr|L'Histoire du très-noble et chevalereux prince Gérard, comte de Nevers et la très-virtueuse et très chaste princesse Euriant de Savoye, sa mye}}.{{sfn|Warrack|1976|p=282}}|name=French romance}} which premiered at the Kärntnertortheater in 1823 to much praise.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="2. Life, 1817–26"}} Weber's fame from ''Der Freischütz'' led to another important commission, this time from the [[Royal Opera House]], London.{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="2. Life, 1817–26"}} For this he composed his final opera and only one in English, ''Oberon'', to a libretto by [[James Planché]], based on [[Christoph Martin Wieland|Christoph Martin Wieland's]] epic [[Oberon (poem)|poem of the same name]].{{sfn|Brown|2002a|loc="Works"}} The work received much acclaim. title: Shōwa-shinzan (昭和新山, Shōwa-shinzan) is a volcanic lava dome in the Shikotsu-Toya National…
description:
Shōwa-shinzan (昭和新山, Shōwa-shinzan) is a volcanic lava dome in the Shikotsu-Toya National Park, Hokkaido, Japan, next to Mount Usu. The mountain was created between 28 December 1943 and September 1945.[2] Initially, a series of strong earthquakes shook the area, and wheat fields were rapidly uplifted. Lava broke through the surface and the current peak was created. The peak is now 398 m (1,306 ft) tall, and still actively smoking.

The name Shōwa-shinzan means “Shōwa new mountain”, as it formed during the reign of Emperor Hirohito, known as the Shōwa period. When Shōwa-shinzan first appeared, the Japanese authorities were worried that it might be interpreted as an unlucky wartime omen, and its existence was kept secret.

I feel if a new mountain appears and you worry that it’s a bad omen, you probably already had an accurate sense of how the war was going…

title: AI has young writers between a rock and a hard place
description:
Buzzwords, clichéd phrases, formulaic sentences, and most notoriously—the use of the em dash. These are all signs readers and writers alike have learned to look out for when trying to spot whether something was written by AI. 

Authors and journalists have faced the brunt of this trend, with accusations of AI use increasing as AI becomes more normalized. Tools can sniff out artificial intelligence, but they can be imperfect and unreliable. 

Between discouraging allegations and increased scrutiny over common writing practices, young writers are beginning to lose motivation, even as their level of AI adoption may vary. According to the Society of Authors, 20% of fiction writers and 25% of nonfiction writers stated that they use AI. But 65% of fiction writers and 57% of nonfiction writers believe AI will hurt their future income from their creative work. 

Alex Del Cueto, a recent college graduate who is an arts journalist at Broadway World, a theatre news website, says he’s concerned about entering the workforce during the rise of AI. “I feel like the rise of AI and its effects [have] made being a young journalist almost impossible,” he says. The growing use of the technology has complicated an already difficult job market in an already competitive field.  

Thanks to AI, young writers are left in limbo. They’re simultaneously struggling to figure out if they need to use AI to keep up in today’s competitive industry—or eschew it altogether in order to maintain trust. (Em dashes and all.)

AI can damage reputation—and mental health

Amid prompts to chatbots being left behind in published books and AI creating fake quotes used in articles, distrust has grown between the audience and writers. In this new world where readers don’t know who (or what) is doing the writing, anything can set off alarm bells for the audience: a new word, offbeat punctuation, or even the content itself. 

People have taken to calling anything they don’t like AI. Whether it’s a book, a photo or video, or an article, “that’s AI” is being used as an insult rather than a legitimate accusation. This can lead to harassment of the creator and a deleterious domino effect on creatives. 

Writers who have been falsely accused of using AI in their writing, for example, have voiced anxiety and disappointment when they come across the negative review. Instead of critiquing nuanced parts of the writing, commenters just throw out the accusation and call it a day. 

In addition to being bad for their mental health, this trend can be extremely harmful to people’s careers. Younger writers have voiced fears of losing a job they don’t even have yet to AI. 

Some writers are now shying away from using language and punctuation that has become associated with AI, like saying something is “X, not Y,” an LLM go-to. For instance: “Using AI isn’t cheating. It’s leveraging resources.”

So instead of developing the fundamentals of their craft, writers can be left focusing on whether their work sounds like it could be written by a bot. “What if I use the em dash too much?” or “Will people believe that I really organically use that word?” start taking over. 

Barb Kay, a student at Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at the City University of New York, says using AI can be a stigma for writers. And seeing it used in methods of research, or to help write a story, can feel discouraging for the writers themselves. 

“I feel discouraged by the implementation of AI in the newsroom and am skeptical of my colleagues who use it,” she says. “While I try to keep an open mind, the harm it does to the environment, and the risk of losing human connection and journalistic integrity, outweigh any benefit it might have.” 

And yet, some writers may still use it 

Despite the stigma and risks, AI is here to stay—and many professionals, including writers, may use it for a variety of purposes. That decision isn’t always born out of laziness or lack of creativity. Sometimes it’s a last resort. 

Some authors who have been accused of AI have admitted to using it to edit their work due to busy schedules, balancing parenting and other jobs, or important responsibilities. Others work independently, and don’t have the budget to pay a real editor to look over their work. 

This isn’t only an individual issue, but a media issue; as the United Nations communications department points out, traditional media outlets are under financial strain. Newsrooms with smaller staffs under pressure to meet traffic targets may prioritize output over quality. 

Creative fields are already hard to break into. So some writers feel the need to take matters into their own hands. 

Platforms like River AI, where writers can use AI to edit and proofread big projects like books, have become more popular. As a result, the number of self-published books has increased for fictional titles in recent years. 

Where does this leave young writers? 

Freelancers or authors with no publishing deal to rely on may be short on money, putting them under intense competitive pressure in a competitive industry. Those who are anti-AI may feel a pull towards using it to vie for an audience, produce material quickly, or gain traffic. 

Another graduate student journalist at Craig Newmark, Natalie Tulloch, says she’s seen newsrooms, both academically and professionally, suggest using AI to take on research tasks. And she wonders why. She feels confident that the research AI can conduct, a human could do better. 

“I think it’s a scary thing, but the more I get [close] to entering the workforce, the more it makes me want to be even better, to prove that AI can’t replace me,” she says.

The human condition of writing

The rise of AI will continue to affect up-and-coming writers. 

Although younger generations report higher levels of skepticism when it comes to the harm AI may cause, the number of young adults using AI keeps increasing. Some media outlets and publishers have tried to combat growing misinformation and alert readers when AI has had a hand in work. 

In March 2026, the Authors Guild allowed authors to add an official certification (the “Human Authored Certification”) to their books in the United States. This would be proof that a book was entirely written by a human, and that minimal to no AI writing tools were used for assistance. Since this option arrived, thousands of authors have employed it in an attempt to distance themselves as much as possible from potential accusations. 

Belle Martinelli, who works as a member services coordinator at the Greater Olean Area Chamber of Commerce in New York while freelancing as a journalist, says the people around her “treat me like an alien” when she tells them she doesn’t use AI. 

“I’m a writer. I love to write,” she says. “I go out, and I report, and I come back and I write. If you can’t do that without a robot you have no business being a journalist . . . because journalism is more than just pen-on-paper writing. It’s about telling stories, telling information, but it’s about moving people. You can’t move people as a robot.” 

When we use AI for creative work that a human can do, we risk undermining the editing process. If human decisions are replaced by AI, the writing will feel more disconnected. The way a writer connects with their audience is crucially human. Only a person can tell another person’s story, fictional or factual, in a way others can relate to and understand. 

That’s simply not something technology can replace.

title: Fosi  Audio  MC331
description:
I've been struggling a bit putting together a sound system for the new print shop space.  Now that it's shared with Bones In Jars, we needed something a little bigger than the Soundburger + Model 1 setup used in the old space and I wanted to offer more source options than only radio and vinyl since we'll be sharing the system now.

I tried using a very weird little class-d + Bluetooth amp I've used for awhile in the lab coupled with an ancient but durable pair of Realistic bookshelf speakers (Minimus 7?) but for some reason this amp doesn't sound right with the Soundburger.  The setup sounded good with a Bluetooth source, but when playing a record something was up with the high-end.  I thought maybe it was some kind of interaction between the amp's line-level input and the 'burger's built-in preamp so I added a buffer in the form of an old mixer I had handy.  This helped, but it still was a bit off and added a lot more hardware to the system than was needed.

I would normally consider a vintage amp/receiver for this, but since the Soundburger doesn't need a phono stage and Bluetooth input is desirable I more or less skipped this option (I did find some interesting Carver's on Ebay but they were in need of repair and I need something that works yesterday).  So I went shopping for something new and after looking at a lot of disappointing and often expensive options, I stumbled upon the Fosi Audio MC331.

I've never auditioned any Fosi gear before, and I've heard a number of small, cheap, class-d  hybrid tube amps that sound like the tubes are just for decoration so I was suspicious that the MC331 was just another one of these.  But after a couple hours of reading reviews and digging-up technical details (as well as becoming more familiar with Fosi's reputation) I decided it was worth giving the amp a shot.



When it arrived I was immediately impressed with the build quality of the little amp.  I've used a number of small class-d power amplifiers and while some have sounded quite good, they have all been rather flimsy, delicate things.  The Fosi is small but substantial, much heavier than expected and that's something considering that the power supply is external to the chassis.  I worried that it would squirm when I tried to adjust the knobs or would get pulled-around when I attached some cables to it but after hefting it in my hand those concerns disappeared.

Setting up the amp consists of little more than connecting the usual input and output cables and power supply with the addition of socketing the tubes.  It was a little funny to me that this felt just like working with tubes on an amp from 50 years ago (I guess I thought maybe tube base/socket tech had advanced some since then).  



Once the tubes were carefully seated I connected the amp to a pair of baby Advents I restored a couple years ago and put it through it's paces with a short but diverse set of music using the Bluetooth input.


Not only is the VU meter cool, it's practical and accurate as well.

I was really impressed with how well the amp drove these speakers.  Being sealed they can be a little power hungry but the little Fosi outshined any other amp I've used with them in terms of loudness.  The quality of the sound was excellent as expected in the mids and highs but I was even pleasantly surprised by the amount of bass kick the amp could summon from the Advents when I cranked-up the Bass knob.

After this initial test I carefully (the tubes are exposed) packed-up the amp and took it down to the print shop to see if it would solve the problem I've been having with the Soundburger.  I'm happy to report that it did, and even coupled with the smaller, cheaper Realistic speakers it sounds damn good.

This alone makes the MC331 worth the (surprisingly low for a tube amp!) price.  There's a lot more to like about it (wide-range of input types, remote control, preamp out, etc.) but all that is covered by other reviews and the owner's manual.  The only thing I might add is a subwoofer to add some kick to the little Realistics, but with a larger set of bass reflex speakers that probably wouldn't be necessary.  That said, I'd love to see Fosi offer this same hybrid configuration with a 2.1 power section and/or a dedicated subwoofer output from the preamp.

If you're in the market for a nice sounding amp for a desktop system or small room I highly recommend the MC331.  I'm probably going to pick one up for my work desk at home and use the USB-C input with my work computer so I can use a cord with my headphones instead of having to either listen to music over Bluetooth or switch back-and-forth when I have to take phone calls.


Jason J. Gullickson, 2026

title: Apple and Amazon users: Beware this new ‘unauthorized charge’ scam
description:
It seems like hardly a month goes by without some new or increasingly frequent online scam trying to separate us from our money or data. In June, it was the so-called Apple High Alert scam. Now it’s a swindle using both Apple and Amazon as its facade. Here’s what you need to know about the Apple and Amazon “unauthorized charge” scam—and how to protect yourself.

What is the Apple and Amazon “unauthorized charge” scam?

The scam is a phishing scheme designed to get unsuspecting targets to hand over their personal details and/or money. Phishing is the practice scammers use to impersonate legitimate organizations in hopes of extracting sensitive information or payment details from you.

The scam involves displaying a malicious pop-up in your browser that purports to be a notification from Apple or Amazon. The scam was recently highlighted by the cybersecurity firm Malwarebytes, which says the scam is delivered by compromised websites, browser redirects, or malicious ads that take a user to a website that looks like Apple’s or Amazon’s in the background. In the foreground, a pop-up will appear that matches the design language of Apple or Amazon.

The pop-up warns that a suspicious pre-authorized payment of $149.99 has been detected on your Apple or Amazon account. It then directs you to call the phone number shown in the pop-up if you did not authorize the charge, to speak with an Apple or Amazon representative, ostensibly to protect your account.

How does the scam work?

The scam works by following certain design and psychological principles.

On the design side, the pop-ups are meant to look like legitimate ones you would see from Apple or Amazon (with rounded corners and blue buttons on the Apple decoys, for example). These pop-ups also have a transparent background that shows what is apparently Apple’s or Amazon’s real website behind them, though this is usually just a screenshot or a cloned site. The point is, the pop-ups are designed to make things look as genuine as possible.

Then come the psychological tricks. The scammers know that most people have an Apple or Amazon account, which means if you see a notification from either company, you are likely to pay it at least some attention. Once the fake notification has your attention, it uses the usual phishing tricks: creating a sense of urgency by claiming that your account or payment method may be compromised and that you need to act immediately, often by calling a phone number, to protect it.

Of course, if you call the phone number, you’ll actually be talking to a scammer who will try to extract personal details from you, like your login, password, payment details, name, address, or more. Alternatively, the scammer may try to get you to make a payment with a credit card or gift card to “protect your account.”

As Malwarebytes notes, the suspicious $149.99 charge that the notification warns about also holds psychological sway. It’s a realistic amount for a product sold on Amazon or a yearly subscription sold on Apple’s App Store. The plausible amount gets you to lower your defenses, making you think, What if this is legit?

How do I know if I am the target of the “unauthorized charge” scam?

The best way to know if you are being targeted by the scam is to pay attention to where the supposed notification appears. 

You should be suspicious of any notification that suddenly appears in your web browser, regardless of whether it’s on mobile or desktop. As noted by Malwarebytes, Apple and Amazon don’t alert you about account or payment issues via browser pop-ups. They’ll send you emails, in-app notifications, or activity log alerts in your account instead.

Another big tell is that the pop-up notifications often direct you to call a phone number, which Amazon and Apple won’t do. You should also be on the lookout for any doom-mongering messaging in the alert, such as threats that failure to act can leave you financially or legally liable. These are frequent tells that the notification isn’t genuine, no matter how authentic it looks.

How can I protect myself against the scam?

Never click on a web-browser pop-up that alleges to be an urgent notification telling you that your account or payment details were compromised. 

If there is actually an unauthorized pending charge on your Amazon or Apple account, those companies likely won’t be the only ones who know about it—your bank or credit card company will, too. So if you see a notification that says someone is trying to make, or has made, a payment you didn’t authorize, you can simply check with your bank or credit card company to see if any charges are pending. You can also close your browser, navigate to Apple or Amazon’s real website, log in to your account, and see any pending charges there.

Finally, often you can easily identify that a notification is a scam by noting the phone number it tells you to call, then simply Googling that number or entering it into one of the many online tools that track scam numbers, like Scamwise or Malwarebytes’s Scam Number Check website.
